nameStory: David's spurge gets its name from the botanist who first described it scientifically, following the common botanical tradition of honoring researchers with species names. The "spurge" part comes from the old word "spurgen," meaning "to purge," referring to the plant family's historical use as a strong laxative. It's also called toothed spurge because of the small teeth along the edges of its leaves.
description: David's spurge is a small annual herb that grows up to 2 feet tall, making it one of the medium-sized members of the spurge family. Like all spurges, it produces a milky white sap when broken and has tiny, inconspicuous flowers. This plant has a somewhat weedy appearance with narrow to broadly oval leaves arranged in pairs along its stems. It's quite rare in New England, with only a couple of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stem with narrow to broadly oval blades that have small teeth along the edges, feeling slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: An upright annual herb reaching up to 2 feet tall with branching stems that feel somewhat succulent when squeezed

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, greenish flowers clustered in small groups that lack showy petals and are easy to overlook among the foliage

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Produces a thick, milky white sap when stems or leaves are broken - this latex-like substance is characteristic of all spurges

habitat: David's spurge is extremely rare in New England and typically found in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil and may appear in gardens or agricultural areas as an occasional weed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin developing their characteristic opposite leaves, growing rapidly in warm weather.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach full size and produce their small, inconspicuous flowers. This is the best time for identification when all features are visible.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to decline and set seed before dying back completely as an annual species.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain as this annual plant completes its life cycle and dies with the first hard frost.

funFact: David's spurge is so rare in New England that it has only been documented twice in the entire region, making it one of the most elusive plants you could possibly encounter on a nature walk - finding one would be like discovering botanical treasure!
confusionNotes: David's spurge can be confused with other small spurges, but its opposite leaf arrangement and toothed leaf edges help distinguish it from most relatives. The milky sap is a dead giveaway that you're looking at some type of spurge rather than an unrelated plant.
contextualKnowledge: All spurges contain a milky latex sap that can be irritating to skin and eyes, so it's best to observe rather than handle these plants. Despite their innocent appearance, many spurges have been used medicinally throughout history, though they can be toxic if consumed.
compareHints: Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs. It's larger than most of the mat-forming sandmat spurges and lacks the showy bracts of species like snow-on-the-mountain. The combination of opposite, toothed leaves and medium height makes it fairly distinctive among New England spurges.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
